Invasion of the Body Snatchers BY JODY DUNCAN F or director Jon Favreau, a mild curiosity about the intriguingly titled Cowboys & Aliens - a film project based on a 2006 graphic novel, which was under development at DreamWorks - grew into real interest after a chance encounter with screenwriters Roberto Orci and Alex Kurtzman at 2009's Comic-Con, where he was promoting the 2010 release of Iron Man 2. "I'd thought that the title was compelling," Favreau recalled, "but I didn't know much about it. And then I ran into Bob and Alex, who were just finishing the script, and they sent it to me to read - and I connected with it immediately. That is rare. Usually you read a script and you can see the potential of it; but, in this case, it was all there. The tone was just rightii The screenplay related the story of an alien invasion of a small western town - Absolution, Arizona - in the year 1873, and the classic western-style counterattack against the invaders by a small band of cowboys, led by reformed gunslinger Jake Lonergan (Daniel Craig) and powerful rancher Woodrow Dolarhyde (Harrison Ford). It was Invasion of the Body Snatchers meets The Searchers ...War of the Worlds meets The Magnificent Seven.

"I knew from the outset that this movie would have to make sense as both genres," stated Favreau. We couldn't say, 'We're making a sci-fi movie, so we don't have to worry if it doesn't work within the logic of a western.' The trick was to respect both genres by playing it straight - not satirizing one or the other or both. The original script played it straight, and that would have to continue with the performances, the casting, the effects, the music, and the editorial style. It was squarely on my shoulders, as the director, to nudge each of those elements one way or the other so that the film maintained the right tone." berg, included Brian Grazer and Ron Howard of Imagine Entertainment. The first order of business was to design the alien. Legacy Effects, with whom Favreau had worked on his previous three films, would build the practical version for use on set; but supervisor Shane Mahan made an impassioned case for letting his creature team design the alien, as well. "My pitch to the studio," said Mahan, "was: 'This is what we specialize in. Creatures - that's what we do.' There have been shows in the past where we've inherited designs, where they just hand you something, and say, 'Here's the alien.' That's fine; but in this case, given our history with the people involved, I said: 'Let our team take a crack at this. You keep referencing films like Predator and Aliens, and those are films that we did with Stan Winston! So why not let us design the alien? If you don't like it, COWBOYS & ALIENS hile still in postproduction on Iron Man 2, Favreau committed to the project, and began meetings with Cowboys & Aliens' slate of heavyweight producers, which, in addition to DreamWorks' Steven Spiel-

you can take over.' They welcomed that approach." COWBOYS & ALIENS Awarded the assignment, Legacy artists - led by Scott Patton and lan Joyner, with Simon Webber playing a key role - started by creating a range of alien designs in Photoshop and 3D modeling packages. "In a week," recalled Scott Patton, "five of us came up with 67 different concepts. "Designs ranged from elegant to insectoid to wormlike," added lan Joyner. "Some were multi-legged, some were two-legged, and some had no legs at all. One of the underlying ideas was that it would be a kind of organic Transformer, with limbs that would emerge from other parts of the body. That Transformer idea was the basis for the little arms that come out of the chest, which was in the final design." Jon Favreau had suggested that the alien have some characteristics of a sea turtle; and so the designers incorporated hard shell-like areas atop an underlying translucent skin in a late-stage digital sculpt. That digital model also had features meant to ensure that the alien would not look like a man in a suit - very narrow hips, and arms that were not only longer than those of a human, but also had hollow areas with bladders that 'breathed.' The creature's height of eight feet would also work against its looking like a man in a suit, and was large enough to appear threatening in relation to characters on horses. 'We wanted to make sure that the aliens weren't dwarfed by people on horseback," noted Favreau. "I wanted them to be a real physical threat, like the aliens in preCG films like Alien, Aliens and Predator.i Using the final digital sculpture, Legacy 'grew' a rapid prototype maquette in its 3D printer. "We painted that," Shane Mahan commented, "and presented it to the producers

COWBOYS & ALIENS as a scaled model. It had separate heads showing different expressions, as well as the opened chest section. It really helped to give them an idea of exactly what this alien was going to be." With the digital design approved, Legacy produced a full-scale version in foam. "We did some cleaning up on that," said Mahan, "and then did a mold and produced a clay version so that we could detail the surface even more. We made traditional molds and ran skins to make it as light and yet durable as possible. It was a combination of silicone joints and urethane shells, and also foam rubber in some areas and fiberglass in others, with a central mechanical frame that everything pinned to. It also had interchangeable heads that we grew in our 3D printer. Arms were rod-puppeted, and the body was on a manually driven motion gimbal and cart. Legacy also equipped the puppet with eyes that could bug out from the alien's face, and a chest piece that irised open, and from which emerged smaller arms and hands.Those little arms were rod puppets, as well, with mechanical fingers." It would take eight to nine Legacy puppeteers - Chris Grossnickle, Johnnie Spence, Hiroshi Ikeuchi, Marc Freeman, Cory Czekaj, Jamie Grove, Mark Killingsworth, Jim Kundig and Christopher Swift - to fully operate the full-scale puppet on set. There was one person on each function," Mahan noted. "One each for the head, neck, mouth, arms, chest, fingers, breathing and the body rig. And then, if a foot came in, we had an additional operator on that. Prior to joining the production, Mahan organized a weekend shoot at Legacy's studio to commit to video the range of performance that could be obtained from the two hero puppets.iWe shot as much of the storyboards as possible

to educate Jon and crew as to what they could expect to get from the character on set. Often you don't have time to do that sort of thing; but in this case, we had beaten the clock, and so we had time to rehearse and do this video. The test we shot was really exhilarating and fun. My daughter Caroline was even there, turning the lights on and off to make 'lightning' for us. We edited that together and showed it to about 30 production people. It was a real confidence builder for them.i W were overseeing animation tests to determine how the computer animated alien would look in ambulatory form against desert landscapes. "We scanned Legacy's maquette and rigged it to give us a digital version of the alien that we could move around inside the computer," Guyett said. "We mocked up a simple environment made up of rocks and some desert terrain, and had the alien moving in that environment. It was pretty crude, but it captured the essence of the alien and what it was going to look like in the shots." Guyett and Chu also choreographed combat vignettes to illustrate what the aliens would look like in confrontation with cowboy characters mounted on horses. "We animated some cowboys and horses and came up with little action scenarios, said Marc Chu.iWe had an alien jumping off a cliff to attack a cowboy on a horse. We had cowboys riding through a canyon, getting ambushed by aliens. By doing these little stories, COWBOYS & ALIENS hile Legacy was building the practical alien, Industrial Light & Magic visual effects supervisor Roger Guyett, who served as the film's overall visual effects supervisor, and ILM animation supervisor Marc Chu

COWBOYS & ALIENS we started to learn the physical language of the alien." Another purpose of the tests was to determine if the animation should be driven by motion capture or keyframed. "The alien is more or less humanoid," observed Chu, ¿so we did some motion capture tests very early on, just to see if we could get some of the movement that way. I took some of our animators down to our motion capture stage and captured some walk and run cycles and general motion -jumping over things, attacks, leaps, things like that - and those tests revealed that motion capture wasn't the way to go. Once we put a human motion on that rig, it just ended up looking like a human. So we determined that this creature should be keyframed. The animation tests also revealed a need for minor alterations to the Legacy design. 'There are always problems with a design that you can't know about until you actually start to move these creatures," Chu stated. "For example, the initial design had a very narrow foot with a singular, pointed claw. But we found, once we started animating it, that we couldn't get a sense of the alien having good purchase with that type of foot. So at ILM, our art and model departments did some work to redesign that foot and parts of the leg." Presented to Favreau and the producers, the animated vignettes helped to earn the film its official greenlight. With that - and with the completion of Iron Man 2 - Favreau turned his full attention to Cowboys & Aliens, meeting with department heads such as Roger Guyett, production designer Scott Chambliss and director of photography Matthew Libatique. Favreau also dove into storyboarding and previzing key sequences with Dan Gregoire of Halon Entertainment.

Whether it is the lens flares in Close Encounters or showing the western landscape in a western, anamorphic lenses have brought something to those genres. So I was very excited about working in that format, as well, and so was Matty Libatique. Anamorphic would give the movie a classic feel that would be true to both genres." Production shot Absolution exteriors at Bonanza Creek Ranch, originally a forced-perspective western town set laid out with smallerscale buildings at one end of a main street and full-scale buildings at the other end. Scott Chambliss and his construction crews rebuilt much of the town, removing and rebuilding the forced-perspective elements, adding new facades to many of the existing buildings and erecting additional structures. The exterior town set served for some interior scenes, as well, such as those inside the saloon and the sheriff's office. ILM enhanced a plate of the location for the initial reveal of the town in the distance, from Jake's POV. "Early on," said ILM visual effects co-supervisor Eddie Pasquarello, "we did a version of the shot where we added a lot of enhancements to the town; but eventually we went back to the original plate and painted out the modern-day stuff and added subtle matte-painting enhancements to give it more life. It does not take long for Jake to find trouble in Absolution, primarily with Percy Dolarhyde (Paul Dano), Woodrow Dolarhyde's bullying son. Dolarhyde's ranch is the setting of the first alien attack in the film, when a chaotic flurry of bright lights and COWBOYS & ALIENS owboys & Aliens begins with Jake awakening in the desert - wounded, disoriented, his memory gone and a strange metallic band inexplicably affixed to his wrist. After fighting off bounty hunters, Jake steals one of their horses

The sequence begins with a flash of light that sends one of the hands falling backward into the stream. "All of this mayhem is happening above him," remarked Eddie Pasquarello, ¿but we're not quite sure what's going on. The audience is going through what the characters are going through, and so the attack is purposely very confusing and vague. And, of course, it is a total mystery to these characters because they've never even seen an aircraft, let alone an alien aircraft." ILM augmented extremely bright rock-concert-style lighting used on location to simulate the attack. "The practical light wasn't enough," said Pasquarello, "so we added digital lighting effects. There's also all this dust that is kicked up, which we enhanced with particle effects and comped smoke elements. With all the additional lighting, particle effects and smoke, we were able to make it look like one continuous blast that was much bigger than what we got on the shoot. ILM composited in brief impressionistic flashes of aircraft flying overhead, as seen from the ranch hand's POV under the water. The character then emerges from the stream, only to find large-scale devastation all around him. ¿The aftermath of the attack was an elaborate matte painting and composite with CG fire and burning cows. That was all done in digimatte. With the exception of the foreground characters, we replaced everything that was in the plate. Environmental and safety regulations limited the scale and number of practical pyrotechnics that could be shot on location, and so ILM created most of the fire effects for this and other alien attack sequences using its proprietary Plume software. Our

Plume tool is so good," said ILM digital production supervisor Michael DiComo, "we went right to it for fire that required any kind of interactivity. Plume allows us to control the scale, the speed, everything. We have a massive stock library of great fire elements we've shot in the past; but to have total control, we use Plume.i For a subsequent sequence in which the aliens attack the town, special effects supervisor Dan Sudick and his team were able to orchestrate a significant number of large-scale explosions on the set; but the town attack still required dozens of visual effects shots, and was one of four centerpiece action and effects sequences in the film. glimpses of what is transpiring outside as alien aircraft - dubbed 'speeders' by production - fly in and discharge their light-emitting weapons, ravaging the town. The craft also shoot out long bolo-type tethers, with grappling hooks at the ends, which wrap around victims and hoist them into the sky. While Dan Sudick's team orchestrated practical explosions and massive laser lighting setups on location for the town attack, stunt coordinator Tom Harper had provided wire rigs to lift actors and stunt people into the air for the alien abductions. "For the most part," said Roger Guyett, "we were able to capture those abductions on location, using a counter-balance type of rig that pulled the actors or stunt people off the ground and up to a height of about 30 to 40 feet. COWBOYS & ALIENS Though the majority of speeder shots in the town attack and throughout the film would be executed by The Embassy, ILM took the creative lead on the speeder, modeling the digital asset to match art department designs and practical versions built by Legacy Effects. "The speeder was a curious beast," commented ILM CG supervisor Robert Weaver, who was instrumental in the look development of the alien craft. "It had five wings, which had lights on them and could spread like a dragonfly's wings, and it had an arching-back capability. Although it was an aircraft, it looked and acted something like a creature; and so, when the audience and the characters first see it, they don't know that there's an alien piloting it. For all anyone knows, the speeder is the alien." Like all the alien hardware, the speeder had been designed to look like something made by a technologically advanced culture, but with properties that would easily blend into 19th-century southwest environments. Stainless steel or slick, titanium-type finishes were rejected in favor of a more industrial-age look.iWe made a shader for the speeder based off anisotropic materials," Weaver explained, "so it had a metallic look, but with direction and depth, which we created through fine scratches and brushed-aluminumtype details. We added specularity to it, but it didn't have an overall bright sheen, which would have looked out of place in the desertiạ In addition to modeling the speeder, ILM animated key shots - led by animator Andy Wong - and lit and rendered them to give The Embassy a target to shoot for. As fantastic a craft as it was, Jon Favreau wanted the speeder's flight animation to be based on real-world reference. We referenced jet maneuvers such as banking to make the speeder animation look like it was grounded in a physical realityii explained Marc Chu,

'and then, beyond that, we added a level of character to it, to make it clear that this COWBOYS & ALIENS wasn't just a normal plane. It was quite an exploration to figure out how to make the speeder feel like an organic flying machine. For example, we had to determine what it would do when it was about to attack. We came up with this curling motion it would do just before it shot out a bolo and grabbed somebody down below. We worked closely with Jon to come up with that language; and then we passed that along to Embassy. The Embassy delivered 70-80 speeder shots, each of which required its team to reshade and relight the ILM asset to accommodate the company's XSI - rather than Maya-based - pipeline. "All the textures were there," said Embassy visual effects supervisor Winston Helgason, ibut we had to reshade the speeder to make ours match to ILM's. We also did some work to redesign the bolo. I think production was worried that the original bolos looked too much like stunt wires that had not been painted out properly. So we added a light system running along the length of the bolo, and put a lensflare effect on the hooks to give them a more interesting look. Embassy artists also did digital double work for the abductees, augmenting practical wirework that had been done on set by Tom Harper and his crew. ¿That was pretty complex character animation because we had to match to the stunt double's work, and everything had to line up and track perfectly." A key Embassy shot in the town attack sequence is set inside the jail wagon. As the attack progresses outside, Jake's wristband - called the blaster - suddenly opens, projecting a holographic heads-up display that artists at ILM designed. "It was hard to come up with a new take on the heads-up display," recalled Eddie Pasquarello. "It was

a high-tech, alien weapon, but it had to be something that would make sense to Jake in the 1870s, and also make sense to the audience. We came up with a fairly simple design for the hologram, based on a gun site, because that was something Jake would understand. Jon was very clear that everything had to make some sense to the characters of this time and place. For example, the bolo that grabs people was something that they would understand because it was similar to a lariat, and yet it suggested a sophisticated technology. There always had to be that marriage of 1870s reality and future alien tech." opening," said Winston Helgason, "we had to replace his arm from the elbow down with a digital arm and blaster, complete with interactive lighting effects. The lighting was complicated because there were explosions and strobe lights from the lasers outside shining on his arm. About 200 frames into the shot, we did a transition back to his real arm wearing the practical open blaster." Now aware that his wristband is a lethal weapon, Jake aims it at a speeder and brings it down in a crash. On location, Roger Guyett rolled cameras as Dan Sudick's team pulled a speeder-shaped mandrel through dirt to create a 30-yard-long trench representing the craft's path as it plows through the landscape. At the end of the trench was a practical crashed speeder fashioned by Legacy Effects, with flashing lights and COWBOYS & ALIENS roduction had shot the jail wagon scene with Daniel Craig wearing a prop blaster in an opened position, and with interactive light from the heads-up display shining on his arm. To actually show the blaster closed and then

COWBOYS & ALIENS smoke effects. "Our job," related Eddie Pasquarello, "was to animate the CG speeder coming in, and line up the crash to the on-set trench. Making sure that we matched into the practical element at the end made those composites tricky. To pump up the shots, ILM added digital dust kicking up behind the crashing speeder, as well as a digital heat trail. Jake and other townspeople cautiously approach the crashed speeder, and discover strange alien footprints tracking away from it, alerting them to the fact that 'something' is out there. The next day, Jake, Dolarhyde, Ella (Olivia Wilde) - a stranger in town who claims that her people, too, have been abducted by the aliens - and other townspeople form a posse to find and destroy the alien invaders. A stop at the log cabin he once shared with Alice stirs flashes of memory in Jake. Matty Libatique achieved the look of this and other flashback sequences via reverse-process, shooting on negative and then processing it as a positive. ILM started with that reverse-process footage, and then enhanced it digitally or - in some cases - created the look from scratch in the computer. During the flashback, a light beam creates a hole in the cabin roof and melts gold coins sitting on a table. The molten gold then flows upwards, out the ceiling opening. Molten gold, achieved as a CG effect by ILM, would be featured more prominently in the film's third act. As reference, the effects team looked at footage of ferrofluid, a liquid metal that is easily manipulated in the presence of magnetic fields. We wanted the molten gold to have an otherworldly look," explained Michael DiComo, "and we thought this ferrofluid was good reference for that. Using magnets, you can almost make ferro-

fluid act. You can make it jump from one magnet to another, form into spikes - all kinds of things. So that was the inspiration for these molten gold effects, which were created through painstaking particle effects work done by our effects CG supervisor Dan Pearson and his team. They pulled out all the tricks for that - fluid sims, surface meshes, fields to attract and repel stuff and noise to randomize it. We also did a lot of different render passes and comp treatments to make these 'fluidy' renders look like they had a hot core to them; and then we added heat displacement, heat ripples and smoke that had interactive light on it from the bright molten metal. that he could shoot on location, in the appropriate lighting.iHalf the problem of an effects shot is trying to re-create the live-action lighting environment, asserted Guyett. So we photographed the riverboat model right there on the day, setting up a parallel feed between two cameras so Jon could see the riverboat model superimposed in the background of a shot as we were lining it upi At New Deal, supervisor lan Hunter oversaw the building of the riverboat miniature. Alien Concept Designs The Alien's description in the script was fairly loose and undefined purposefully, so it gave our concept team an open invitation to create the look and feel of the the Aliens per the director and producers notes and comments. Scott Patton and lan Joyner produced a myriad of images to choose and modify as meetings progressed. The main thing that Jon Faverau wanted was a bee hive colony approach with little in terms of wardrobe or external weaponry. The size of the Aliens was determined by After the main ideas were solidified a maquette was created and a full size creature the height of a man on a horse for battle sequences. was underway. Click "Play" button to see Alien Concept Art Slideshow

Alien Puppet Construction The construction of the alien started with a full size mill in foam of the approved miniature 3D model. Initial molds were made and clay patterns and sculpts were finished off by a team of Legacy sculptors. Experiments with various urethanes and silicones were conducted to best suit the lightweight yet strong exterior shells of the alien were made and shown to the director. Skin colors were created as well showing colors that would look good in daylight as well as interior dark sets. Two full size animatronic Aliens supplied the full movement rigs as well as one Actor driven upper torso. Ten dead aliens were made to populate the landscape and a series of contact puppets were made for attack scenes. Click "Play" button to see Alien Puppet Construction Slideshow

Alien Speeder & Torture Table Props The Legacy team produced two full size versions of the Speeder (the craft the aliens fly in to collect people during attacks scenes) and also built two dissection tables used within the alien cave mines. These designs were created by production designer Scott Chambliss and his team and a digital model was supplied that Legacy 3D artist Josh Herman re-modeled so that practical parts could be milled in foam. The model department, headed up by Dave Merritt, scratch built much of the detail on the speeder based on Chambliss's original concepts. Many paint surfaces were made to show various ideas to the director until it was decided to give it a metal based look. The attack crafts were made of various resins and metal structures working within the molds and internal lights were fed through the wings. Dan Sudicks team created a massive movement gimbal to which Legacy could attach the Speeder. Click "Play" button to see Speeder & Torture Table Slideshow

cinefex Jake comes face to face with the 'über-alien, an intellectually superior creature that conducts experiments on human captives. Though similar in appearance to the alien soldiers, the über-alien featured a larger head and translucent skin.

cinefex Jake fires on the gold machine, causing its contents to spill onto the über-alien. As reference for the molten gold effects, ILM artists studied footage of ferrofluid, a liquid metal that is easily manipulated into different shapes via the influence of magnetic fields. The final effect employed fluid simulations, generating fields to attract and repel specific areas, and adding noise to randomize the look. The creature's fiery demise involved multi-layered composites comprised of the regular CG uber-alien, a burnt version, and liquid ore effects manipulated to flow down the alien's body and then harden into a rigid gold shell.

HARRY POTTER he film ends with a scene set in King's Cross Station, 19 years later, as harry, off on their first year at Hogwarts. The task of aging 19- to 21-year-old actors into their late thirties was a daunting one for makeup effects. "We did it twice," stated Nick Dudman. ¿The first time was on location at Kings Cross. To prepare for that, Martin Rezard did a series of digital concepts, and makeup department head Amanda Knight and I discussed what we could achieve with color and makeup. We knew it had to look real; it could not jump off the screen as makeup. We did tests using tiny prosthetics. For the girls, we used little roll-on platgel appliances; but for them, it was more about hairstyles and costume. For the boys, we took their hairlines back fractionally with a forehead piece, gave them little jowls, eye bags, and tiny nasolabial folds. We made body suits for all of them. The girls were fractionally thicker in the middle. The boys we made slightly stockier, but not so you'd really notice. It couldn't be obvious what we'd done." After the location shoot, Dudman reviewed footage with David Yates, and the filmmakers realized the illusion was not working. "David was very magnanimous," said Dudman. "He wasn't happy with the way he'd shot the scene; he felt he had tried to make too much of a statement, aging them too far. It was a perfect storm where we were not quite there with everything. So we decided we'd shoot it again." Knowing that the scene was integral to Harry's story, and beloved by fans, the production knuckled down and built a replica of a portion of King's Cross, which was no longer available, and resolved to augment the set with visual effects. John Richardson's team assisted in

HARRY POTTERI positioning the 75-ton Hogwarts Express locomotive on set, rigging a bulldozer, cables and pulley system to create the impression of the engine, plumbed with steam, beginning to shunt out of the station. Makeup effects were revised to employ minimal roll-on platgel appliances and a lessspecific attempt at aging the characters 19 years. "It's a hideous age to hit," Dudman observed. Some people don't seem to change at all, and other people change dramatically. What it boiled down to was augmenting the performance. Any more than that, and it was heading towards arrogance. Our final makeups were only noticeable by comparing before-and-after photos; it was bloody difficult to tell what we did. The production filmed characters and extras in a partial platform set with greenscreen backings. Framestore added digital extensions, created from photographic and painted textures projected onto 3D geometry, plus a scattering of magical characters, including a CG chocolate frog and airborne origami birds. After a test screening, the production elected to further augment age treatments, returning to Lola Effects in the final months of postproduction. We did facial deformations to make characters' faces sag around their skulls," said Edson Williams. "We lengthened nose tips, extended earlobes, added jowls, made necks a little wider, thinned out upper lips. We added crow's feet in the corners of their eyes - that was in the makeup, but we pushed it a little further - and we warped skin under the eyes to give that a little bit more droop. We enhanced Harry's five-o'clock shadow to make him a little gruffer. Ron we gave more girth, made his earlobes bigger, darkened his eye-bags and gave him a slightly more bulbous nose-tip. For the girls, we took the saturation out of their lips, increased the

pores of their skin, added furrows to their brows, and made the hair less vibrant. It was all the cues of aging, but done subtly so it did not appear to be a visual effecti The production's in-house compositing department generated the final fade to black on a medium shot of Harry, Ron and Hermione, with a vignetting effect momentarily lingering on Harry's face as other characters faded out. The shot had special significance for its compositor, whose experience with the series dated back to years at Cinesite and Mill Film. "I'm quite proud to say that I've worked on every Potter film," recalled Michael Illingworth. 'That includes a shot on the first film where Dumbledore used a deluminator spell to switch off lights outside Harry's house on Privet Drive. That was one of the first visual effects shots in the first film; and then I did the final shot of the final film. Studios' new 170-acre film production site. cinefex The final confrontation between Voldemort and Harry takes place in Hogwarts' devastated courtyard. David Yates filmed the sequence on a Leavesden backlot set, which production designer Stuart Craig conceived as significantly larger than previous Hogwarts courtyards. Double Negative supplied architectural extensions, layered in background terrain derived from Scottish scenic textures, and added a matte-painted sky. Cinesite provided Voldemort nose replacements, and MPC created wand effects - animated with a powerful new fluid simulation system - that preserved the color palette of wand blasts seen in previous Potter films.

cinefex The destruction of each Horcrux causes the erosion of the Dark Lord's powers. Nick Dudman's team manifested Voldemort's deterioration with subtle bruising and broken skin effects in Ralph Fiennes' makeup, which Cinesite incorporated into the digital nose prosthetic. As Harry gains the upper hand in the duel, forcing dark magical energy back toward Voldemort, Double Negative extended the Hogwarts terrain and MPC generated wand effects retracting into Voldemort's wand.

cinefex For Voldemort's death at the hands of the young Harry Potter, MPC tracked Fiennes' performance and fashioned effects showing the Dark Lord's eyes glazing over, and his flesh withering and flaking away.

cinefex Nineteen years later, the three wizard friends - now in their late thirties - meet at King's Cross to send their children off on their first year at Hogwarts. After extensive testing of prosthetic makeup effects with Nick Dudman, and an earlier location shoot that revealed the aging effects as being too extreme, the production reshot the scene on a partial set at Leavesden. Dudman's team refined the prosthetics, using ultra-fine silicone appliances and subtle body padding. Framestore created set extensions derived from photographic surveys of King's Cross, and Lola Visual Effects further augmented age makeups with subtle digital effects.
